_changelog: v1.0.0 (2026-10-16) first version. Concepts are the catalog's w12 slugs (composite-pattern, trees), both already listed in catalog v1.0.120. Title and setting from the Workshop bible v1.0.1 row w12 (the catalog's w12 entry has no setting field; its lld title is In-memory file system). w11 has no file yet, so there was no tease to honour; this case follows the bible row. next says the Workshop is finished, as the brief asks. Prerequisites list season cases only (s5e04 for classes, objects and methods; s5e06 for design patterns); earlier Workshop cases are mentioned in prose only. The bible's three wrong ideas are kept: a depth limit of 100 on the size walk, a list of folders already counted kept by the size report only, and ask users to be careful (left as Gruffudd's first answer in Odgerel's reply to the copy-then-delete comment, not an option, since the fourth slot is the warn option). The bible's numbers for the hook (22:50 drag, 01:00 report) are kept; all sizes, the 2,000 MB printer limit, the 200 MB a second copy speed and the bench's 1,000-folder stop are given data the sim states and reproduces. Every name was chosen after the name lookup and a scan for names inside names (Brochfael, Gruffudd, Yrsa, Phelim, and the handle endings hroald and ulfhild); candidates that clashed, or held a shorter name inside them, were dropped before drafting, so no name in this file was renamed. The 1994 book's authors are not named here (s5e06 names them), so no real person's name repeats.
title: The Folder Inside Itself

post.author: u/workshop_nights_odgerel
post.title: I finish my late great-aunt's machines at night. Her print-queue program for a sign shop hung at 01:00, and on the screen one folder now sits inside its own subfolder.

blocks.text: My great-aunt, Winifrith Torvaine, built coin-operated machines and clockwork figures for sixty years, and in her last ten wrote small programs for local shops. She died in the spring and left me her workshop. I'm Odgerel, a night-shift programmer; I finish her jobs in the evenings, each with a paper work order tied on.

blocks.title: WORK ORDER 12. Brochfael Signs, the night print run.
items: Finish the print queue: the folders of print files our big printer works through at night.
Folders hold files and other folders. Every folder must report its total size.
At 01:00, size every job on the run sheet. No job over 2,000 MB (megabytes): the printer can't hold it.
Then start the run. Staff move folders by dragging them on the screen.

blocks.text: Brochfael Signs prints banners overnight on a printer as wide as a door. Each customer's job is a folder of print files. File sizes are counted in MB, megabytes; one MB holds about a million letters. The program keeps every folder in the computer's memory, its fast working space.

Folders inside folders branch out from one top folder, like a family tree drawn downwards. Programmers call that shape a tree. Every folder or file in it has exactly one parent: the folder it sits in.

Winifrith wrote it as classes, patterns for one kind of thing in code. Here is the part I finished; each line names a class or step, then what it holds or does. File(Item) means a file is one kind of Item. A folder keeps a list of its children, the items inside it:

Item          name, parent, size()
File(Item)    size() = its own MB
Folder(Item)  children; size() = walk below it
Tree.move(item, target)
  take item out of item.parent's children
  put item into target's children
  set item.parent to target

Asked its size, a file gives its own MB. A folder walks everything below it with a to-do list: first it puts itself on the list; then it takes one folder off, adds up its files and puts its subfolders on; it repeats until the list is empty.
Tree.move is what a drag does: drop an item on a folder, the target, and move takes it out of its old folder, puts it in the target and points its parent there.
The run sheet lists the night's jobs, each as a link straight to the job's folder, like a bookmark, wherever it sits.

On Wednesday 14 October at 21:40, Yrsa, the night print operator, put three jobs on the run sheet: bakery-menus, harbour-fest and ferry-times. The festival job is two banners and a subfolder of test prints, proofs. At 22:50 Phelim, a designer, dragged harbour-fest from drafts towards ready, the folder for finished jobs. On the crowded screen it landed on proofs, open just below. No message came up.
At 01:00 on Thursday the size report began. Each line shows the time, the job and its total:

01:00:00  size report, 3 jobs
01:00:00  bakery-menus     46 MB
01:00:00  harbour-fest     counting...

Nothing more. At 01:20 Yrsa found the printer idle and rang me. The folder list, which starts from the top folder, no longer showed harbour-fest. Opened from the run sheet, it showed proofs; inside proofs, harbour-fest; inside that, proofs again.
The folder list had lost it. The run sheet still found it, and it had no bottom.
I came in, put harbour-fest back in drafts by hand, and the run started at 02:10, in time for Saturday's festival. Nobody had ever dropped a folder into its own subfolder before.
Winifrith's notebook has one pencil line beside the program: *Before you hang a thing up, ask the hook what it hangs from.* The run goes out again tonight. What should I change?

blocks.label: folders_2251_redrawn.png

diagram.aria: The print queue just after 22:50. The top folder, queue, holds ready and drafts. Ready holds bakery-menus, 46 MB, and ferry-times, 64 MB. Drafts held harbour-fest until 22:50, drawn dashed. The folder harbour-fest, with 760 MB of files, holds proofs, with 24 MB of files, and since 22:50 proofs also holds harbour-fest, drawn as a red arrow back up. The run sheet's link still points straight at harbour-fest.

blocks.caption: I redrew the folder list as it stood just after 22:50. Each arrow points from a folder to an item inside it. At 22:50 harbour-fest left drafts and went into proofs, which sits inside harbour-fest, so the two now hold each other, and nothing above them leads down to them any more. The run sheet's link still points straight at harbour-fest. Going down from there, the walk goes harbour-fest, proofs, harbour-fest, proofs, and never runs out of folders.

comments.author: u/grey_pager
comments.text: Draw the folders twice, at 22:49 and at 22:51, and write each one's parent and children. After the drag, start at the top folder and follow children down: what can you reach? Now start at the run sheet's link and do the same with the to-do list. When does the list run empty? A path that comes back to where it started is called a loop. A tree makes one quiet promise: going down always ends. Your move's three lines change the tree. Which of them makes sure the promise still holds? And size isn't the only thing in that program that walks down a folder.

replies.author: u/workshop_nights_odgerel
replies.text: Right: the run sends each job to the printer by walking its folder the same way, file by file, with the same to-do list. Everything in the tree hangs off the top folder, queue.

comments.author: u/hundred_levels_hroald
comments.text: Every walk over a tree should have a depth limit. A level is one step down, from a folder into a subfolder, counting the job folder itself as level 1. Your jobs are 2 levels deep at most. Make the size walk stop going down after 100 levels, and the report always finishes, whatever staff drop where. One line, done by tonight.

replies.author: u/workshop_nights_odgerel
replies.text: Gruffudd would rather fix the report itself: keep a list of the folders it has already counted, and skip any folder it meets again. Then every folder is counted once, loop or no loop.

comments.author: u/copy_then_delete_ulfhild
comments.text: I'd change move instead. Make it copy the item into the target first, then delete the old one. The copy has to walk down through every item in the folder it copies anyway, so let it watch for the target on the way. If it meets the target down there, the target is inside the folder: it stops and refuses, and the old folder stays where it was.

replies.author: u/workshop_nights_odgerel
replies.text: Copying in memory runs at about 200 MB a second on the shop's computer, and until the old one is deleted the memory holds both. Gruffudd's own first answer was simpler: tell staff to be more careful.

reply.prompt: The run goes out again tonight. What should Odgerel change before then? Part 2 follows your advice.

options.text: Make the size walk stop going down after 100 levels, so every count comes to an end.
options.verdict: A finished count, a false number
options.part2: I put harbour-fest back and capped the size walk at 100 levels. On the bench, Wednesday's slip: the report finished at 01:00, but only after going round until the cap, 50 times through harbour-fest and 50 through proofs, so it said harbour-fest was 50 x 784 = 39,200 MB. That is over the printer's 2,000 MB, so the run skipped it. On the night of Friday 23 October a drag slipped again: Phelim dropped ferry-times onto winter, its own subfolder. At 01:00 on Saturday the report said ferry-times was 3,200 MB, fifty times its real 64 MB, and the run printed the other jobs and skipped it. Yrsa found the ferry company's timetables unprinted in the morning, and ferry-times was missing from the folder list until I put it back by hand.
options.senior: A depth limit turns a walk that never ends into a walk that ends with a wrong answer, and a wrong answer that looks like a number is worse than a hang. The tree is still broken: the folder is still cut off from the top, and every other walk that has no cap still goes round. Limits are a fair safety net for walks over data you don't control, but the fix is to keep the tree a tree, at the one place that changes it.

options.text: Refuse a move if the target is the item or inside it: walk up the target's parents.
options.part2: I put harbour-fest back and made move check before it changes anything. First it looks at the target: if that is the item being moved, it refuses. If not, it steps up to the target's parent and asks again, until it passes the top folder. On the bench, Wednesday's slip: proofs is not harbour-fest, but its parent is. Refused after 2 checks, with a message on the screen: a folder can't go inside itself. Dropped into ready, as Phelim meant, it checks ready, then queue, 2 checks, and the move goes through. On the night of Friday 23 October the slip came again: Phelim dropped ferry-times onto winter. Refused after 2 checks; Phelim dragged it again, more carefully. At 01:00 on Saturday the report gave three totals and the run started on time. The check costs one step per level above the target: 2 for each of these drops.
options.senior: Every walk in the program trusts one promise: going down always ends, because each item has one parent and nothing leads back up. Keep that promise where the tree changes, not in every reader. Walking up from the target costs one step per level, and the parent links make it possible. POSIX systems such as Linux put the same rule in their rename call, so a directory can't be moved inside itself.

options.text: Make move copy into the target, then delete the old one; a copy won't go into itself.
options.part2: I made move copy, then delete. On the bench, Wednesday's slip: the copy walked down harbour-fest, met proofs, the target, and refused; nothing moved. On the night of Friday 23 October Phelim's slip with ferry-times was refused the same way, and the run started at 01:00 on Saturday. But every move now copies everything inside. Dropping harbour-fest into ready, as Phelim meant, copies 784 MB at 200 MB a second: 3.92 seconds of a frozen screen, and the memory holds two harbour-fests until the delete. Phelim asked why dragging had gone sticky. And if the program stops between the copy and the delete, the queue wakes up with the job twice.
options.senior: It is safe, because the copy can never place a folder inside itself. But it pays for the check by walking and copying everything below the folder, so the cost grows with the folder's size, where looking up from the target costs only its depth. It also needs room for two copies and leaves two copies behind if the program stops halfway. Copy-then-delete makes sense between two separate stores; inside one tree, a move should only relink.

options.text: Have the size walk skip any folder it has already counted, so each counts just once.
options.verdict: Fixes one reader, not the tree
options.part2: I put harbour-fest back and gave the size report a list of folders already counted. On the bench, Wednesday's slip: it counts harbour-fest, then proofs, meets harbour-fest again and skips it: 784 MB, right, and the run starts at 01:00. Then the run sends harbour-fest to the printer, walking the same folders without the list: banner-1.tif, banner-2.tif, proof-a.pdf, proof-b.pdf, banner-1.tif again, and on. On the night of Friday 23 October Phelim's slip put ferry-times inside winter. At 01:00 on Saturday the report said 64 MB, and the run printed the other jobs, then summer.pdf, winter.pdf, summer.pdf, winter.pdf, until Yrsa saw a third summer timetable come out and stopped the printer. A roll of paper went in the bin, and ferry-times was still missing from the folder list.
options.senior: Guarding one reader leaves every other reader exposed: the print sender, the folder list, a backup, a delete. A list of what you've seen is the right tool when the data really is allowed to loop, such as links between web pages. A folder tree is not allowed to loop, so stop the loop where it is made, in move, and every reader stays simple.

sim.title: Run Wednesday's drag through the print queue
sim.lede: You're Odgerel at the workbench, replaying Wednesday 14 October from 21:30:00. The queue: the top folder, queue, holds ready and drafts. Ready holds bakery-menus (menu-board.pdf, 46 MB) and ferry-times (summer.pdf, 28 MB, and a subfolder, winter, with winter.pdf, 36 MB). Drafts holds harbour-fest (banner-1.tif and banner-2.tif, 380 MB each, and a subfolder, proofs, with proof-a.pdf and proof-b.pdf, 12 MB each). At 21:40 Yrsa puts bakery-menus, harbour-fest and ferry-times on the run sheet; at 22:50 a drag. At 01:00 the size report sizes each job; if it finishes, the run sends every job of 2,000 MB or less to the printer, in run-sheet order, by walking its folder. Copying runs at 200 MB a second. The bench can't wait forever: it stops any walk after 1,000 folders and calls it never-ending. Pick the drag and a design.
sim.tryThis: Try this: press Step twice and watch harbour-fest land in proofs. Play the rest: the report never finishes. Change the drag to ready, as Phelim meant. Back on the slip, try the depth limit and read the total; then the counted-folders list and watch what the printer gets. Try Friday's slip with ferry-times. Last, try copy-then-delete and the walk up the parents, on all three drags.

explain.oneLine: Nothing in the files was wrong. Move put harbour-fest inside its own subfolder, so the two folders held each other: cut off from the top, still linked from the run sheet, and with no bottom for the size walk to reach.

steps.title: What move did at 22:50.
steps.text: First, move took harbour-fest out of its old parent, drafts. Second, it put harbour-fest into the target's children; the target was proofs, which sat inside harbour-fest. Third, it set harbour-fest's parent to proofs. Each line did exactly what it says. Nothing asked whether proofs was below harbour-fest. Now harbour-fest held proofs and proofs held harbour-fest: a loop. And because drafts no longer held it, nothing going down from the top folder could reach either folder. That is why the folder list lost it.

steps.title: Why the report never finished, and why it started there.
steps.text: The size walk ends when its to-do list is empty, and on a tree it always empties, because every step goes one level down and the levels run out. Here, first the walk put harbour-fest on the list. Second, it took it off, added 760 MB of banners and put proofs on. Third, it took proofs off, added 24 MB and put harbour-fest on, again. The list never emptied, and the total kept climbing. The folder list starts at the top, so it never met the loop; the run sheet's link goes straight to harbour-fest, so the 01:00 report walked right into it, and the run waits for the report.

steps.title: The composite pattern, and the promise it relies on.
steps.text: Winifrith's design is the composite pattern: files and folders share one type, Item, so any code can ask any item its size without checking which kind it is. A file, the leaf, answers with its own MB. A folder, the composite, asks each child and adds up the answers, and a child folder does the same in turn. It is like asking a box how heavy it is: it weighs its own contents and asks each smaller box inside. The pattern quietly relies on the shape being a tree: each item has one parent, and nothing below a folder leads back to it. Then every walk down ends. Break that once, and every walk that goes down, the size, the printer's sender, a delete, can go round for ever.

steps.title: Keep the promise where the tree changes: walk up from the target.
steps.text: A loop can only be made by moving a folder below itself, so check that in move, before anything changes. First, start at the target. Second, if it is the item being moved, refuse. Third, step to its parent and ask again. Fourth, when you pass the top folder without meeting the item, the move is safe: do the three lines. Wednesday's slip is refused at the second check, proofs then harbour-fest. The cost is one step per level above the target, a handful, whatever the folders hold. What can go wrong: a parent link that is out of step with the children list, so keep both changed together in move, and nowhere else.

diagram.aria: The fix, walking up from the target. Wednesday's slip drops harbour-fest onto proofs. Check 1: proofs is not the item. Check 2: its parent, harbour-fest, is the item, so the move is refused. A drop onto ready, as meant, checks ready, then its parent, queue, reaches the top without meeting harbour-fest, and is allowed. Each arrow points from an item to its parent.

explain.caption: The fix, drawn for tonight. Each arrow points from an item up to its parent. Before move changes anything, it starts at the target and walks up. Wednesday's slip, onto proofs: check 1, proofs is not harbour-fest; check 2, its parent is, so the move is refused and nothing changes. Phelim's meant drop, onto ready: ready, then queue, the top, without meeting harbour-fest, so the move goes ahead.

fix.title: The fix: refuse a move into the item itself or below it, by walking up from the target
fix.text: Before Tree.move changes anything, start at the target and walk up its parent links to the top folder. If any step lands on the item being moved, refuse the move and say why on the screen: a folder can't go inside itself. Otherwise take the item out of its old parent's children, put it into the target's children and set its parent, all in move and nowhere else, so the parent links and the children lists always agree. Keep the size walk and the run's sender as they are: on a tree they always end.

limits: The check only protects changes that go through Tree.move. A repair tool, a test or a hand fix that sets a parent directly can still make a loop, so make move the only way an item changes folder.

Walking up trusts the parent links. If a parent link and a children list ever disagree, the walk checks the wrong path, so change both together in one place, and check they agree when the program starts.
Some data really may loop, such as shortcuts that point at other folders. If the queue ever gets shortcuts, the walks that follow them need a list of folders already seen, as well as this check.

head: Design
Good
Bad
rows: Three simple lines; right for every drop that lands somewhere else.
A drop into its own subfolder makes a loop: the report never finishes, the run never starts.
Wrong totals: harbour-fest 39,200 MB, ferry-times 3,200 MB, so the run skips real jobs; the loop stays.
The report's totals are right: 784 MB.
The run's sender still goes round, printing the same files again; the folder list still can't find the job.
No loop can be made; a bad drop leaves everything where it was.
Every move copies all its MB: 784 MB in 3.92 seconds, double memory meanwhile, two copies if it stops halfway.
No loop can be made, at one step per level above the target.
Every move must go through Tree.move, and parent links must stay in step with children lists.

explain.seniorTake: When code walks a structure, it relies on the structure's shape: a tree promises that going down ends. Decide what shape your data must keep, and enforce it at the one place it changes, not in every reader. Readers that each defend themselves, with depth caps and seen-lists, multiply, disagree and turn hangs into wrong numbers. Parent links earn their keep here: the question 'is this target below the item?' becomes a short walk up, one step per level. The same idea shows up as an org chart where a manager can't report to their own report, a category tree, nested comment threads and permission groups inside groups. And the composite pattern only stays elegant while the tree really is a tree.

realWorld.title: POSIX rename(): no directory inside itself
realWorld.text: The POSIX standard's page for rename() (IEEE Std 1003.1-2024) says "The old pathname shall not name an ancestor directory of the new pathname." Its list of errors gives EINVAL for when "The old pathname names an ancestor directory of the new pathname," the same rule as Odgerel's fix, kept by the operating system's own move.

realWorld.title: Linux: rename(2)
realWorld.text: The Linux manual page for rename says "rename() renames a file, moving it between directories if required." Its EINVAL entry reads "The new pathname contained a path prefix of the old, or, more generally," and goes on: "an attempt was made to make a directory a subdirectory of itself."

realWorld.title: The composite pattern's intent
realWorld.text: A pattern catalogue that credits the 1994 book Design Patterns gives the composite's intent as "Compose objects into tree structures to represent part-whole hierarchies." and "Let clients treat individual objects and compositions of objects uniformly." Files and folders answering size() alike is that.

realWorld.title: Parent links and saved totals
realWorld.text: The same catalogue page notes that "sometimes the Component may need to know the Composite that contains it (if any)." That is the parent link. It also says "The Composite may contain a cache to store information on the sum of components it contains.": a saved total, which then has to be kept right when items move.

asked: How would you represent files and folders so that both can report their size?
How do you stop a folder from being moved inside itself?
interview.answer: Start with one shared type, a node, with a name, a parent link and size(). A File is a node that holds its contents and answers size() with its own length. A Folder is a node that holds a map from name to child node, and answers size() by asking each child and adding the answers: the composite pattern, so callers never need to check which kind they have. Keep a root folder, and find a path by splitting it on slashes and stepping down one name at a time. Operations: make a folder, write and read a file, list, delete, move. Move is where the shape is kept: before changing anything, walk up from the target through parent links to the root; if you meet the node being moved, refuse, because that would put a folder inside itself and make a loop. Otherwise unlink it from its old parent's map, link it into the target's, and set its parent, all in one place so the links and maps always agree. Walking up costs one step per level, the depth of the target, so it is cheap. If sizes are asked for often, a folder can keep a saved total, but then every change must update the totals of every folder above both the old and the new place, again by walking up. Mention the limits: shortcuts that can point anywhere break the tree promise, and walks that follow them need a seen-list. And two moves at once can each pass their check and still make a loop together, so let only one move run at a time, with a lock.

terms.def: The workshop Winifrith Torvaine left to Odgerel: half-finished coin-operated machines and clockwork figures, each with a paper work order tied on and a program to match.
A machine that works when you put a coin in, such as a ticket machine.
A paper slip saying what a client wants made or finished. Work order 12 is Brochfael Signs': finish the print queue, signed by Gruffudd.
The sign shop in this story. Gruffudd runs it, Yrsa is the night print operator and Phelim a designer.
The person who runs the big printer at night. Yrsa puts the night's jobs on the run sheet and watches the run.
The folders of print files the printer works through. Its top folder, queue, holds ready (finished jobs) and drafts (jobs in progress).
The night's list of jobs to print. Each entry is a link straight to a job folder, like a bookmark, wherever the folder sits.
The night's printing: after the size report, the program sends each job on the run sheet to the printer, file by file.
Test prints for a customer to check before the real job. In harbour-fest, a subfolder holding proof-a.pdf and proof-b.pdf, 12 MB each.
A measure of how much data a file holds: about a million letters' worth. The two banners in harbour-fest are 380 MB each.
A computer's fast working space, where a running program keeps what it is using. The print queue's folders live there.
Folders and files kept in a program's memory as a tree, rather than on the computer's own disk. The print queue is one.
A shape where everything branches out from one top item, like a family tree drawn downwards. Each item has exactly one parent, and nothing below an item leads back up to it.
One thing in the tree, a file or a folder. Item is the shared type both are kinds of; programmers usually call an item in a tree a node.
The folder an item sits in. Every item keeps a link to its parent; the top folder has none. Not the same as s5e04's parent class.
The items inside a folder. A folder keeps a list of them.
A folder inside another folder. proofs is a subfolder of harbour-fest.
The one folder everything else hangs from: queue. It has no parent.
How far down an item sits: one level per step from a folder into a subfolder. Hroald counts the job folder itself as level 1.
A pattern for one kind of thing in code, like a blank form (s5e04). Item, File and Folder are classes.
One real thing made from a class, like one filled-in form (s5e04). Each folder in the queue is a Folder object.
A set of steps a class can carry out, such as size() or move() (s5e04).
The method that asks an item how big it is. A file gives its own MB; a folder walks everything below it and adds up the files.
Going through every folder below a starting one: take a folder off the list, deal with its files, put its subfolders on, and repeat until the list is empty.
What a drag does: take the item out of its old parent's children, put it into the target's children, and set its parent to the target.
The folder an item is dropped on, so the folder it is moved into.
Moving something on a screen by holding it with the mouse, carrying it over a folder and letting go.
A pointer straight to one thing, like a bookmark. The run sheet holds links to job folders, so it finds them wherever they sit.
The view on the shop's screen that starts at the top folder and shows what is inside each folder, going down.
The 01:00 step that sizes each job on the run sheet and checks it is 2,000 MB or less, the most the printer can hold. The run waits for it.
A path that comes back to where it started. After the slip, harbour-fest held proofs and proofs held harbour-fest: going down never ended.
A rule that a walk stops going down after a set number of levels, such as 100. It ends every walk, but a loop then gives a wrong total.
A list a walk keeps of folders it has visited, so it can skip one it meets again. Also called a seen-list or visited set.
Moving by copying the item into the target, then deleting the old one. The copy walks down through every item it copies, so it can spot the target below.
Start at the target and follow parent links up to the top folder, checking each folder on the way. It costs one step per level.
A design pattern (s5e06) where single things and groups of things share one type, so code treats them alike; a group answers by asking its parts. Files and folders here.
In the composite pattern, a leaf has no parts (a file) and a composite holds parts (a folder). Both are kinds of the shared type.
Things made of smaller things, which are made of smaller things again, like boxes inside boxes. A folder tree is one.
The 1994 book by four authors that named the composite pattern, among many others (s5e06).
An item's ancestors are its parent, its parent's parent and so on up to the top; its descendants are everything below it.
A folder's size, worked out once and kept, so it can be shown without walking. It must be updated whenever anything below the folder changes.
A standard, IEEE Std 1003.1, describing how Unix-like operating systems behave, including the rename() call that moves files and directories.
The main program that runs a computer and looks after its files, such as Linux. Its own move call keeps files and folders in order.
The operating system's word for a folder.
A rule in a program that lets only one piece of work through at a time, like a single key to a room. Two moves at once would each wait for it.
A question asked of a database, the program that stores a business's records. One that follows parents down a tree walks it, like size().
rename() is the operating system call that moves or renames a file or directory. EINVAL is the error it gives for a bad request, such as moving a directory inside itself.
A folder or file's full address, the names of the folders from the top down to it, such as queue/drafts/harbour-fest.
Odgerel's workbench: the sim, which replays Wednesday's night, with the drag and the design you pick.
The sim can't wait forever, so it stops any walk after 1,000 folders and reports it as never-ending, with the total so far.

atWork: Look for trees that people can rearrange: folders in a document store, categories in a shop, an org chart where a manager is moved, nested comment threads, permission groups inside groups. In a database these often sit as a table where each row names its parent's row. Read-only access to the code is enough to check. Find the code that changes an item's parent, and ask: does it refuse a new parent that is the item itself, or anything below it? Then find the code that walks the tree, such as a database query that follows parents down level by level, a size or headcount report, a permissions check, and ask what it does if a loop ever gets in. Fix it at the write: walk up from the new parent before saving, and refuse if you meet the item. If two moves can run at once, let only one run at a time with a lock, or two moves that each pass their check can still make a loop together.

recall.prompt: Your company's staff directory lets managers drag a team under another team. On Monday someone dragged the support team onto one of its own sub-teams. Now the support team has vanished from the chart drawn from the top, and the nightly headcount report, which starts from each team on its own list, has been running for hours. What happened, and what do you change?

keyIdeas.idea: The drag made a loop: the team became a child of its own sub-team, cut off from the top of the chart
The headcount walk starts inside the loop and going down never runs out, so it never finishes
Refuse a move whose target is the team itself or below it, by walking up the target's parents

recall.model: The drag made a loop: the support team became a child of its own sub-team, so the sub-team holds the team and the team holds the sub-team. Nothing going down from the top reaches either, which is why the chart lost it. The headcount report starts from each team on its own list, so it walked straight into the loop, and going down never runs out: it goes round and round. Fix it where the tree changes: before a move, walk up from the target through each parent link to the top. If you meet the team being moved, refuse the move; otherwise relink it. Repair the loop by hand first.

recall.prompt: Phelim drops a folder onto a target. Which check refuses every drop that would make a loop, and nothing else?
options: The target is not the folder's current parent
The target is fewer than 100 levels below the top folder
Walking up from the target, through each parent, never reaches the folder
recall.why: A loop needs the folder to go into itself or something below it, and exactly those targets have the folder among their parents, their parents' parents and so on. The other checks refuse safe drops, let loops through, or both.

recall.prompt: A teammate asks why File and Folder share one Item type in the print queue, instead of two unrelated classes with a separate size function for each. Explain what the shared type buys, what a folder's size() does, and what the design quietly assumes about the shape of the data.

keyIdeas.idea: One shared type lets any code ask any item its size without checking whether it is a file or a folder
A folder's size asks each child for its size and adds the answers up
It assumes a tree: one parent per item and nothing below leading back up, so every walk down ends

recall.model: It is the composite pattern. Because File and Folder are both kinds of Item, any code can ask any item its size the same way, without checking which kind it has; a new kind of item fits in without changing the callers. A file answers with its own MB. A folder asks each child for its size and adds the answers up, and a child folder does the same in turn. The design quietly assumes the data is a tree: every item has one parent and nothing below a folder leads back up to it, so every walk down always ends. A loop breaks that, and then size() never returns.

recall.prompt: Move checks a drop by walking up from the target to the top folder. How much work is that?
options: One step for every item in the whole queue
One step for every level above the target
One step for every file inside the folder being moved
recall.why: Each step goes from a folder to its parent, so the walk takes as many steps as there are levels above the target. It doesn't depend on how much the folders hold. Copy-then-delete, by contrast, walks everything inside the moved folder.

coldCase.update: UPDATE, 3 months later. Move walks up from the target now, and no folder has gone inside itself since. In November Gruffudd asked for each folder's total beside its name in the folder list, so I gave every folder a saved total. Move keeps them right in two steps: take the item's size off its old parent's total, add it to the target's. On the night of Monday 11 January, at 23:15, Phelim dragged a 512 MB job, carnival, out of drafts/2027 into ready. At 01:00 on Tuesday the list showed 2027 at 0 MB and ready 512 MB bigger, but drafts still said 512 MB, and all it holds is the empty 2027 folder.
coldCase.prompt: Reply to OP. Why does drafts still show 512 MB, and how should move keep the saved totals right?

keyIdeas.idea: A folder's total includes everything below it, so a move changes the total of every folder above the old place and above the new place, not just the two parents
Walk up the parent links from the old parent subtracting, and from the target adding, as far as the top folder
Or don't save totals at all and work them out when asked; saved totals are a trade of speed for upkeep

coldCase.model: drafts' total counts everything below it, including what is inside 2027. The move took 512 MB off 2027, the old parent, and added it to ready, the new parent, but never touched drafts, the grandparent, so drafts still counts carnival. queue looks right only by luck, because it lost and gained the same 512 MB from both sides. A move changes the total of every folder above the old place and every folder above the new place, all the way up, not just the parent. So walk up the parent links: from the old parent to the top, subtract the item's size at each folder; from the target to the top, add it. It is the same walk up the move check already does. Or drop the saved totals and work them out when asked, which is slower but has nothing to keep in step: a trade-off between speed and upkeep.
